synthesis.cpt-conjugation-pseudoscalar-r.formal:
Let $\R^{2,4}$ carry the conformal ambient metric, $\Cl(2,4)$ its Clifford algebra with $e_0^2 = e_1^2 = 1$ and $e_2^2 = \dots = e_5^2 = -1$, $I_6 = e_0 e_1 \cdots e_5$ its unit pseudoscalar, and $\Cl(2,4) \otimes \C = \Cl(3,4) = \Cl(2,4) \oplus \Cl(2,4)I_7$ its complexification, whose complex unit is the central pseudoscalar $I_7 = I_6e$ of the odd extension ($e$ orthogonal to $\R^{2,4}$, $Q(e) = +1$; Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}); $\kappa$ is complex conjugation, the automorphism induced by $e \mapsto -e$, which fixes $\Cl(2,4)$ and sends $I_7$ to $-I_7$. $I_7$ is the complex unit throughout; $I_6$ is the real pseudoscalar of $\Cl(2,4)$, which acts on pure spinors with eigenvalues $\pm I_7$, and the two are not identified. Let $W \subset \C^6 = \R^{2,4} \oplus I_7\R^{2,4}$ be a maximal isotropic subspace with $W \cap \overline W = 0$ (the generic Witt flag of Definition \claimref{obj.dark-matter.witt-flag}), and $\psi_W$ its pure spinor.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The composite of grade involution and reversal is an anti-automorphism of $\Cl(2,4)$, not an automorphism, and acts on vectors as $-1$. Grade involution equals $\mathrm{Ad}(I_6)$, and $I_6 = (e_0e_1)(e_2e_3)(e_4e_5)$ is a rotor of the identity component: each factor squares to $-1$ and is $\exp(\pi B_k/2)$, and $I_6 \widetilde{I_6} = 1$. So the vector action $-1$ lies in $SO_0(2,4)$. In $\Cl(1,3)$, by contrast, $I_4\widetilde{I_4} = -1$.
\item $W$ is the $+I_7$ eigenspace of an orthogonal complex structure $J$ on $\R^{2,4}$, $W \oplus \overline W = \C^6$, and $I_6\psi_{W} = \pm I_7\,\psi_{W}$, $I_6 \psi_{\overline W} = \mp I_7\,\psi_{\overline W}$. So $\overline W$ lies in the other family, and complex conjugation is a flag conjugate. In $\Cl(3,3)$, $I_6^2 = +1$ and conjugation preserves the family.
\item Every real-linear isometry $g$ of $\R^{2,4}$ with $g(W) = \overline W$ has $\det g = -1$, so that $\epsilon(gI, gV, gF, gF) = -\epsilon(I, V, F, F)$ for vectors $I, V$ and bivectors $F$, $g$ acting on bivectors by its outermorphism. The complex-linear Witt exchange $v_k \leftrightarrow w_k$ does not preserve $\R^{2,4}$.
\item $C := \mathrm{Ad}(I_6) \circ \kappa$ is an antilinear involutive automorphism of $\Cl(2,4) \otimes \C$ that is $-1$ on $\R^{2,4}$, fixes the metric, $\epsilon$ and $I_6$, and carries $\psi_W$ to a multiple of $\psi_{\overline W}$. With the flag conjugate realised by $\kappa$, the stored composite $\phi$ (grade involution, reversal, flag conjugate) is reversal composed with $C$: an antilinear anti-automorphism. No realisation of the flag conjugate on $\R^{2,4}$ is both real-linear and orientation-preserving.
\item \emph{Convention.} A (possibly anti-) automorphism $\phi$ acts on fields as a symmetry: on a vector field by its vector part, and on a connection $A$ through the Lie algebra automorphism it induces, $A \mapsto -\phi(A)$ when $\phi$ is an anti-automorphism, so that curvature transforms by the same automorphism; for the stored composite this is the action of $C$. In this convention every action functional of real tensor (multivector) fields on which $C$ acts through its vector part, invariant under constant $SO_0(2,4)$ transformations, in particular the frozen point's $Q(I)^{-1}\int \epsilon(I, V, F, F)$ (\claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-makes-stelle-west-vector}), satisfies $S \circ \phi = S$, while with any real-linear flag conjugate in place of $\kappa$ the same action changes sign. Spinor fields are not covered. If instead $\phi$ is applied to the Clifford integrand $IVFF$ as a whole and the top-grade coefficient taken, both sign statements invert (with $\kappa$ the integrand changes sign, with a real-linear flag conjugate it is preserved), so the conclusion of (5) depends on the convention.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.cpt-conjugation-pseudoscalar-r.technical: The seventeenth refutation rests on CPT conjugation, stored as the composite of grade involution, reversal and the flag conjugate $v_k \leftrightarrow w_k$ and described as a real linear automorphism that is not the antiunitary CPT operator of quantum field theory. This result fixes the type. Reversal makes the composite an anti-automorphism. On the conformal ambient its vector part, $-1$, is the action of the pseudoscalar $I_6$, which is a product of three commuting rotations by $\pi$ and so lies in the identity component: unlike in $\Cl(1,3)$, where total reflection needs complexification, here it is a real gauge rotation. What is left is the flag conjugate. For a generic flag $W$ the complex conjugate $\overline W$ is complementary and lies in the other family, because $I_6^2 = -1$ makes chirality an imaginary eigenvalue, so complex conjugation exchanges the families while fixing every real structure. Any real-linear exchange of the families has determinant $-1$ and reverses the frozen point's MacDowell-Mansouri integrand. So, when the conjugation acts on fields as a symmetry (vectors by its vector part, connections through the induced Lie algebra automorphism), the conjugation that leaves the action invariant, as the refutation needs, is antilinear on the complexified ambient and on the Fock module, of Wigner's antiunitary type (argued). Applying the anti-automorphism to the Clifford integrand as a whole inverts the sign statements, so this convention is part of the result. In it the premise's action clause holds for the frozen point's action and for every functional of real tensor fields invariant under constant conformal rotations; spinor fields, the fermionic and the internal gauge sectors remain premised.
synthesis.cpt-conjugation-pseudoscalar-r.lay: The argument that the universe's matter-antimatter orientation is a free choice relies on a symmetry that swaps matter with antimatter and reverses space and time. The series described this symmetry as an ordinary linear operation, unlike the one used in quantum field theory. This result checks the algebra exactly and finds the opposite. In the six-dimensional space the series works in, the space-and-time reversal part is just a rotation, a symmetry the theory already has. The matter-antimatter swap is the genuinely new part, and acting on the fields in the usual way, it leaves the gravitational action unchanged only if it acts by complex conjugation, the same kind of operation quantum field theory uses. Done as an ordinary linear swap, it would flip the sign of the gravitational action.

proofs.main:
\emph{(1) Anti-automorphism and the rotor.} Grade involution $\alpha$ is an automorphism and reversal is an anti-automorphism of every Clifford algebra, and they commute (\claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}), so $\alpha \circ \widetilde{\ }$ satisfies $\alpha(\widetilde{xy}) = \alpha(\widetilde y)\,\alpha(\widetilde x)$; it is not multiplicative, since on $x = e_0$, $y = e_1$ it gives $\alpha(\widetilde{e_0e_1}) = -e_0e_1 \neq e_0e_1 = \alpha(e_0)\alpha(e_1)$. On a vector, reversal is the identity and grade involution is $-1$. The blades $B_1 = e_0e_1$, $B_2 = e_2e_3$, $B_3 = e_4e_5$ commute pairwise and $B_k^2 = -e_{2k-2}^2 e_{2k-1}^2 = -1$ in each case (the products of squares are $(+1)(+1)$, $(-1)(-1)$, $(-1)(-1)$), so $\exp(\theta B_k) = \cos\theta + B_k \sin\theta$ (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}) and $\exp(\pi B_k/2) = B_k$; hence $I_6 = B_1B_2B_3 = \exp(\tfrac{\pi}{2}(B_1+B_2+B_3))$ is joined to $1$ by the path of rotors $\exp(\tfrac{t}{2}(B_1+B_2+B_3))$, $t\in[0,\pi]$, and $I_6\widetilde{I_6} = 1$. In even dimension $I_6$ anticommutes with every vector (\claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}), so $\mathrm{Ad}(I_6)$ is $-1$ on vectors and equals $\alpha$ on the whole algebra (both are automorphisms agreeing on generators). In $\Cl(1,3)$ with $e_0^2 = 1$, $e_{1,2,3}^2 = -1$, $\widetilde{I_4} = I_4$ and $I_4^2 = -1$, so $I_4\widetilde{I_4} = -1$ and $I_4$ is not a rotor; this is the algebraic form of Theorem \claimref{singularity.euclidean-rotor-where-it-lies}(3), that the Euclidean rotation is realised by no real rotor of $\Cl(1,3)$. Checked exactly: anti-multiplicativity on fixed elements, failure of multiplicativity, $B_k^2 = -1$, $I_6\widetilde{I_6} = 1$, $\mathrm{Ad}(I_6) = \alpha$ on generators and on products, $I_4\widetilde{I_4} = -1$.

\emph{(2) The conjugate flag.} If $W$ is maximal isotropic with $W \cap \overline W = 0$ then $\C^6 = W \oplus \overline W$ by dimension; define $J$ as multiplication by $I_7$ on $W$ and by $-I_7$ on $\overline W$ ($I_7$ the complex unit of the formal level). $J$ commutes with $\kappa$, so it is real, $J^2 = -1$, and it is orthogonal: for $x, y \in W$, $B(Jx,Jy) = -B(x,y) = 0$ by isotropy, likewise on $\overline W$, and for $x \in W$, $y \in \overline W$, $B(Jx,Jy) = (I_7)(-I_7)B(x,y) = B(x,y)$. Conversely the $+I_7$ eigenspace of any orthogonal complex structure is maximal isotropic and meets its conjugate in $0$. For the structure $J: e_0 \mapsto e_1$, $e_2 \mapsto e_3$, $e_4 \mapsto e_5$ the eigenspace is spanned by $w_k = e_{2k-2} - I_7e_{2k-1}$, with $Q(w_k) = 0$, $w_aw_b + w_bw_a = 0$, and $w_a\overline{w_b} + \overline{w_b}w_a = \mathrm{diag}(4,-4,-4)$, nondegenerate, so $(W, \overline W)$ is a Witt pair. The null blade $N = w_1w_2w_3$ is annihilated on the left by each $w_k$ and is the pure spinor of $W$ in the left-ideal model, and $\overline N$ that of $\overline W$. Since $I_6$ anticommutes with each $w_k$, $I_6N$ is again annihilated by $W$, hence a multiple of $N$; exactly, $I_6 N = I_7N$ and $I_6\overline N = -I_7\overline N$ (the second is the conjugate of the first, $I_6$ being real). Chirality is the eigenvalue of $I_6$, so $W$ and $\overline W$ are in opposite families, as Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chiralities}(iii) requires of a Witt pair with $m = 3$. Every $J'$ of the same family as $J$ gives the same eigenvalue, by (ii) of that Proposition, so the conclusion holds for every flag with $W\cap\overline W = 0$. In $\Cl(3,3)$, $I_6^2 = (-1)^{15}(+1)^3(-1)^3 = +1$, chirality is real, and conjugation fixes the family; there a flag conjugate cannot be $\kappa$. Checked exactly: isotropy, the Gram matrix, annihilation, the two eigenvalues, $I_6^2$ in both signatures.

\emph{(3) Real-linear exchanges.} Let $g \in O(2,4)$ with $g(W) = \overline W$. Its complex-linear extension is an isometry of $\C^6$ carrying $W$ to a subspace of the other family, so by Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chiralities}(ii) it is the vector action of an odd versor, $\det g = -1$. The integrand $\epsilon(I,V,F,F)$ is the coefficient of $I_6$ in the grade-six part of $IVFF$, a multilinear alternating function of six vector slots, so under the outermorphism of $g$ it is multiplied by $\det g = -1$. An instance is the reflection in $e_1, e_3, e_5$, which carries each $w_k$ to $\overline{w_k}$ and $I_6$ to $-I_6$; on the fixed rational data of the check, $\epsilon(I,V,F,F) = -152$ and its image is $+152$, with or without the composite of grade involution and reversal applied first. The complex-linear exchange $w_k \leftrightarrow v_k$, $v_k = \overline{w_k}/B(w_k,\overline{w_k})$ with $B(w_k,\overline{w_k}) = 2, -2, -2$, sends $e_0 = \tfrac12(w_1 + 2v_1)$ to $\tfrac12 v_1 + w_1$, which has the component $-\tfrac34 I_7e_1$ in $I_7\R^{2,4}$; it does not preserve $\R^{2,4}$.

\emph{(4) The antilinear conjugation.} $\kappa$ is an antilinear automorphism fixing $\Cl(2,4)$ pointwise, and $\mathrm{Ad}(I_6)$ is a linear automorphism with real $I_6$, so they commute and $C = \mathrm{Ad}(I_6)\circ\kappa$ is an antilinear automorphism with $C^2 = \mathrm{Ad}(I_6^2) = \mathrm{Ad}(-1) = \mathrm{id}$. On $\R^{2,4}$ it is $-1$; it fixes $I_6$; it fixes the metric and $\epsilon$ because $-1 \in SO(2,4)$. It carries $N$ to $I_6 \overline N I_6^{-1} = -\overline N$, a pure spinor of $\overline W$. With the flag conjugate realised by $\kappa$, the stored composite is $\widetilde{\ }\circ\alpha\circ\kappa = \widetilde{\ }\circ C$, an antilinear anti-automorphism; on the Fock ideal it sends the left ideal of $W$ to a right ideal of $\overline W$, the dual module, which is the form in which the pairing on the Fock module exchanges grade $k$ with grade $3-k$. A real-linear realisation reverses $I_6$ by (3), and an orientation-preserving one cannot be real-linear by (3), which proves the last sentence of (4). Checked exactly: multiplicativity and antilinearity of $C$ on fixed complex elements, $C^2 = \mathrm{id}$, $C(I_6) = I_6$, $C(N) = -\overline N$.

\emph{(5) The action clause.} In the convention of the formal level, on real tensor fields $\kappa$ acts trivially, so $C$ (and the stored composite, which acts on fields as $C$) acts on every real tensor field of the fibre as the constant element $-1 = \mathrm{Ad}(I_6)$ of $SO_0(2,4)$, by (1); every functional invariant under constant $SO_0(2,4)$ transformations is therefore $C$-invariant. The frozen point's action is $Q(I)^{-1}\int \epsilon(I,V,F,F)$ with $I, V$ fibre vectors and $F$ the curvature, a fibre bivector (\claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-makes-stelle-west-vector}); under $C$, $I \mapsto -I$, $V \mapsto -V$, $F \mapsto F$ (bivectors are even), $Q(I)$ is unchanged and $\epsilon$ is unchanged, so $S \circ C = S$. With a real-linear flag conjugate $g$ the same computation gives the factor $\det g = -1$ by (3). The base manifold is not acted on: $C$ is a fibre map, and its vector part $-1$ fixes every null line (it sends each null ray to the opposite ray), hence acts trivially on the points of the conformal compactification, the projectivised null cone.

\emph{The convention, and what changes without it.} The stored composite $\phi = \widetilde{\ }\circ\alpha\circ\kappa$ is an anti-automorphism. As a symmetry of fields it acts on vectors by its vector part, $-1$ on real vectors, and on a connection $A$ (bivector valued) by the Lie algebra automorphism $A \mapsto -\phi(A)$ that every anti-automorphism induces on the commutator algebra; on bivectors $-\phi = \alpha = \mathrm{Ad}(I_6)$ is the identity, so $F \mapsto F$, which is the action of $C$. Substituting $\phi$ itself into a bivector slot ($F \mapsto \phi(F) = -F$) is not an action on curvature, since $X \mapsto -X$ is not a Lie algebra automorphism; it agrees with the convention on $\epsilon(I,V,F,F)$, which is even in $F$, but not on functionals odd in a bivector field: on the check's data with $E = \langle ab\rangle_2$ for fixed vectors $a, b$, $\epsilon(I,V,F,E) = -226$ is fixed by $C$ and goes to $+226$ under substitution. A different reading applies $\phi$ to the Clifford integrand $IVFF$ and takes the coefficient of $I_6$: then, since reversal is $-1$ on grade six, the composite with $\kappa$ sends $-152$ to $+152$ and the composite with the real reflection $g$ of (3) keeps $-152$. In that reading the sign statements of (3) to (5) invert and a real-linear flag conjugate composed with Clifford conjugation would preserve the integrand. The statements here are made in the field-action convention, which is how a symmetry acts on fields and how the seventeenth refutation applies $C$ (argumentwise); the computed values of both readings are checked.

\emph{What this does and does not settle.} The premise's description of the conjugation as ``a real linear $\mathbb{Z}_2$ automorphism'' is wrong twice as stated, in the field-action convention: with reversal it is an anti-automorphism, and the flag conjugate compatible with the action clause is antilinear. The antilinear automorphism $A \mapsto \Theta A \Theta^{-1}$ of an antiunitary $\Theta$, and the linear anti-automorphism $A \mapsto \Theta A^{*}\Theta^{-1}$, are the two standard forms of Wigner's antiunitary symmetries (literature, from memory: Wigner 1932; the CPT theorem and Jost's result that total reflection lies in the identity component of the complexified Lorentz group, Streater and Wightman, \emph{PCT, Spin and Statistics, and All That}, 1964, ch.~4); the conformal ambient makes that reflection real by (1). This is offered as the identification, argued, not proved. Clause (5) proves the premise's action clause, in the field-action convention, for functionals of real tensor fields invariant under constant $SO_0(2,4)$. It does not cover spinor fields (real quaternionic spinors of $\Cl(2,4) \cong \Mat_4(\HH)$ are real, but $C$ acts on them by $\mathrm{Ad}(I_6)$, which includes a right multiplication and is not a spin transformation), the internal gauge sector or fermions, on which $\kappa$ acts as charge conjugation on the complex module; there the clause is the reality of the action under $\kappa$, and it stays a premise.

synthesis.imported-real-clifford-algebra.formal:
Let $\Cl(p,q)$, $n = p + q$, have orthonormal generators $e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}$ with $Q(e_{i}) = +1$ for $i \le p$ and $Q(e_{i}) = -1$ for $i > p$, and identify $x \in \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ with the blade $e_{x}$, the increasing product of the $e_{i}$ with $x_{i} = 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Twisted group algebra; Ovsienko, after Albuquerque and Majid.) $\Cl(p,q)$ is the twisted group algebra of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ over $\R$ with $e_{x}e_{y} = (-1)^{f(x,y)}e_{x+y}$ and the bilinear twisting function $f(x, y) = \sum_{1 \le j < i \le n}x_{i}y_{j} + \sum_{p < i \le n}x_{i}y_{i}$; the associated quadratic form is $\alpha(x) = f(x, x) = \sum_{j < i}x_{i}x_{j} + \sum_{i > p}x_{i}$, so $e_{x}^{2} = (-1)^{\alpha(x)}$, and its polar form $\alpha(x + y) + \alpha(x) + \alpha(y) = f(x, y) + f(y, x)$ records anticommutation.
\item[(b)] (Ovsienko, Theorem 1.) Two twisted group algebras of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ over $\R$ with bilinear twisting functions are isomorphic if and only if their quadratic forms are equivalent over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$. In particular the classification of the real Clifford algebras is the classification of the forms $\alpha_{(p,q)}$.
\item[(c)] (The Arf invariant; Ovsienko; Elduque and Rodrigo-Escudero.) For nondegenerate polar form the Arf invariant of $\alpha_{(p,q)}$ separates the real matrix algebras (Arf invariant $0$) from the quaternionic ones (Arf invariant $1$); Elduque and Rodrigo-Escudero revisit the classification of real Clifford algebras, with new proofs of classical results, through the Arf invariant of these forms.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Provenance:} \cite{Ovsienko2016}; \cite{ElduqueRodrigoEscudero2018}.
synthesis.imported-real-clifford-algebra.technical: A real Clifford algebra is a twisted group algebra of a vector space over the two-element field: the basis blades are indexed by subsets of the generators, multiplication adds the index sets, and a sign is given by a bilinear function on the index sets. Evaluated on the diagonal it gives a quadratic form over the two-element field that records which blades square to minus one, and its polar form records which pairs anticommute. Ovsienko proved that two such twisted group algebras are isomorphic exactly when their quadratic forms are equivalent, so the classification of real Clifford algebras and that of quadratic forms over the two-element field are one problem, and that the Arf invariant distinguishes real from quaternionic matrix algebras; Elduque and Rodrigo-Escudero revisit the classification through the Arf invariant. Both are taken from the literature.
synthesis.imported-real-clifford-algebra.lay: Whether the products of basic directions in one of these algebras square to plus or to minus one can be written as a yes-or-no table, and published work shows that this table, read as a simple algebraic form, already determines which algebra one has, including whether it is built on real numbers or quaternions. The results are taken from the literature.

synthesis.nilpotent-steps-derivative-exp.formal:
Coefficients and the point $x$ are rational, and $f$ is a rational function with rational coefficients, regular at $x$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The dual-number derivative.)} For any element $n$ of an algebra with $n^{2} = 0$, $f(x + n) = f(x) + f'(x)\,n$; in particular in $\Cl(0,0,1)$, with generator $\rho$, $f(x + \rho) = f(x) + f'(x)\,\rho$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Through a generalised inverse.)} A vector $\rho$ of the radical of $\Cl(p,q,r)$, $r \ge 1$, satisfies $\rho\,x\,\rho = 0$ for every $x$, so it has no generalised inverse and the step in (i) cannot be divided by. If instead $n^{2} = 0$ and $g$ is a generalised inverse of $n$ ($ngn = n$), then $gn$ is idempotent and
\[
g\,\big(f(x + n) - f(x)\big) = f'(x)\,gn .
\]
In the minimal completion, which is nondegenerate and so von Neumann regular, $\rho$ becomes a null vector $n$ with a Witt partner $m$ ($nm + mn = 1$, $nmn = n$), and $m(f(x + n) - f(x)) = f'(x)\,mn$; in $\Cl(1,1)$, for the anti-automorphism exchanging $n = \tfrac12(e_{+} + e_{-})$ and $m = \tfrac12(e_{+} - e_{-})$, the partner is the generalised inverse whose idempotent $mn$ is self-adjoint.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The nilpotent exponential.)} Let $b_{1}, \dots, b_{N}$ commute pairwise with $b_{i}^{2} = 0$, and $\varepsilon = b_{1} + \dots + b_{N}$. Then $\varepsilon^{k} = k!\,e_{k}(b_{1}, \dots, b_{N})$ with $e_{k}$ the elementary symmetric polynomial, $\varepsilon^{N+1} = 0$, and
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1 + b_{i}) \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{\varepsilon^{k}}{k!} \;=\; \exp\varepsilon ,
\]
a finite sum. Such steps with nonzero product exist in $\Cl(0,0,2N)$ ($b_{i} = \rho_{2i-1}\rho_{2i}$), in $\Cl(2N,2N)$ (products of disjoint pairs of $2N$ mutually orthogonal null vectors), and already in $\Cl(N,N)$: for Witt pairs $v_{i}, w_{i}$ and $\pi_{j} = v_{j}w_{j} - w_{j}v_{j}$, the steps $b_{i} = v_{i}\pi_{1}\cdots\pi_{i-1}$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The nilpotent boost.)} In $\Cl(1,1)$ let $B = e_{t}e_{r}$, $Q(e_{t}) = 1$, $Q(e_{r}) = -1$, and $l_{\pm} = e_{t} \pm e_{r}$. For scalars $\alpha, \beta$ and $R = \alpha + \beta B$, $R\,l_{+}\widetilde{R} = (\alpha - \beta)^{2}\,l_{+}$ and $R\,l_{-}\widetilde{R} = (\alpha + \beta)^{2}\,l_{-}$; the boost with $R^{2} = \tfrac54 + \tfrac34 B$ sends $l_{+}$ to $\tfrac12 l_{+}$ and $l_{-}$ to $2\,l_{-}$. Over the ring $\R[d]/(d^{2})$, realised by $d = s\,\rho_{1}\rho_{2}$ in $\Cl(1,1,2)$,
\[
\exp(\tfrac12 dB)\,l_{\pm}\,\exp(-\tfrac12 dB) = (1 \mp d)\,l_{\pm} ,
\]
so a boost of rapidity $d$ scales a null vector by $1 - d$. Here $d$ is a scalar of $\R[d]/(d^{2})$ and $\exp(-\tfrac12 dB)$ is the inverse of $\exp(\tfrac12 dB)$; the reversion of $\Cl(1,1,2)$ fixes the grade-$4$ element $dB$, and conjugation by $R$ and $\widetilde{R}$ with that reversion leaves $l_{\pm}$ fixed.
\end{enumerate}
No limit is removed: derivatives of functions that are not rational, and the exponential of an element that is not nilpotent, still need analysis.
synthesis.nilpotent-steps-derivative-exp.technical: The first-order truncations behind two limits of analysis, the derivative and the exponential, are exact identities when the step is nilpotent; this covers rational functions and nilpotent arguments only. A square-zero step $n$ turns every rational function into its first-order expansion, $f(x + n) = f(x) + f'(x)n$, so the derivative is read off as a coefficient. A degenerate direction cannot be divided by, since $\rho x \rho = 0$ for every $x$; after the completion the step becomes a null vector with a generalised inverse, any one of which turns the difference into the derivative times an idempotent, and the Witt partner is the one with a self-adjoint idempotent. Several commuting square-zero steps multiply to the exponential of their sum, a finite polynomial, because every power of the sum is $k!$ times an elementary symmetric polynomial; such steps are products of orthogonal null vectors in $\Cl(2N,2N)$, and Jordan-Wigner twisted null vectors already in $\Cl(N,N)$. Over the dual numbers a boost of nilpotent rapidity $d$ scales a null vector by $1 - d$, the first-order form of the scaling $e^{-\phi}$; with rational $\cosh\phi = \tfrac54$ the finite scaling is exactly $\tfrac12$.
synthesis.nilpotent-steps-derivative-exp.lay: Calculus usually gets a derivative by letting a step shrink towards zero. In these algebras there are nonzero quantities whose square is exactly zero, and using one of them as the step gives the derivative of any formula built from arithmetic, and the exponential of such a step, exactly; for other functions, and for the number pi, a limit is still needed. Dividing by such a step is impossible in the degenerate algebra, but after the series' repair step the step gains a partner that divides by it as far as possible, leaving the derivative times a projection.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} $x$ is a scalar and commutes with $n$, and $n^{2} = 0$, so $(x + n)^{k} = x^{k} + kx^{k-1}n$ and $u(x + n) = u(x) + u'(x)n$ for a polynomial $u$. For $f = u/h$ with $h(x) \ne 0$, $h(x + n) = h(x) + h'(x)n$ has the inverse $h(x)^{-1} - h'(x)h(x)^{-2}n$, and multiplying gives $f(x) + (u'h - uh')(x)h(x)^{-2}n = f(x) + f'(x)n$. In $\Cl(0,0,1)$, $\rho^{2} = 0$ (Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.radical-ideal-and-quotient}: the radical generates a nilpotent ideal, here with $J^{2} = 0$). The check runs $f = (x^{3} + 3x)/(x^{2} + 1)$, with $f' = (x^{4} + 3)/(x^{2} + 1)^{2}$, at four rational points against hand-stated values.

\emph{(ii)} A radical vector anticommutes with every vector and squares to $0$, so $\rho x \rho = \pm x\rho^{2} = 0$ for every product $x$ of vectors, hence for every $x$; so $\rho x \rho = \rho$ has no solution. If $ngn = n$ then $(gn)^{2} = g(ngn) = gn$, and by (i), $g(f(x + n) - f(x)) = g\,f'(x)n = f'(x)\,gn$. Theorem \claimref{conformal.minimal-nondegenerate-completion} embeds $\Cl(p,q,r)$ in the nondegenerate $\Cl(p{+}r, q{+}r)$, in which $\rho$ spans a hyperbolic plane with a partner $m$; that algebra is regular by Lemma \claimref{transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents}, and for the Witt pair $nmn = n(1 - nm) = n$ (Proposition \claimref{singularity.pseudo-inverse-identities-hyperbolic-atom}; the pair obeys the relations of Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.witt-basis-car}). In $\Cl(1,1)$ the anti-automorphism $\dagger$, reversion composed with $e_{-} \mapsto -e_{-}$, exchanges $n$ and $m$, so $(mn)^{\dagger} = n^{\dagger}m^{\dagger} = mn$; another generalised inverse, $g = m + 3n + 2nm$, has $gn = mn + 2n$, idempotent but not self-adjoint. The check verifies $\rho x \rho = 0$ on every blade for each radical generator of $\Cl(0,0,1)$, $\Cl(1,1,1)$, $\Cl(1,2,1)$, $\Cl(0,0,2)$ and $\Cl(1,3,1)$, and the derivative identity for both $g$ on $2x^{3} + 5x$ at four points and on $(x^{3} + 3x)/(x^{2} + 1)$ at two, against hand-stated values.

\emph{(iii)} The $b_{i}$ commute, so the multinomial expansion of $\varepsilon^{k}$ holds, and every monomial with a repeated factor vanishes since $b_{i}^{2} = 0$; the surviving monomials are the products over $k$-element subsets, each appearing $k!$ times, so $\varepsilon^{k} = k!\,e_{k}(b)$, and $e_{N+1} = 0$. Expanding $\prod(1 + b_{i})$ gives $\sum_{k}e_{k}(b) = \sum_{k \le N}\varepsilon^{k}/k!$, and the exponential series of the nilpotent $\varepsilon$ stops at $k = N$. Realisations: $\rho_{2i-1}\rho_{2i}$ is even, so it commutes with every product of other generators, and $(\rho_{2i-1}\rho_{2i})^{2} = -\rho_{2i-1}^{2}\rho_{2i}^{2} = 0$. Mutually orthogonal null vectors anticommute and square to $0$ (Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.witt-basis-car}), so the same two computations apply to products of disjoint pairs; in $\Cl(2N,2N)$ the vectors $\tfrac12(e_{j} + e_{2N+j})$, $j = 1, \dots, 2N$, are such a family. For the Jordan-Wigner steps in $\Cl(N,N)$: $\pi_{j}^{2} = 1$, $\pi_{j}$ anticommutes with $v_{j}, w_{j}$ and commutes with $v_{i}, w_{i}$ for $i \ne j$, so $b_{i}^{2} = v_{i}^{2}(\pi_{1}\cdots\pi_{i-1})^{2} = 0$, and for $i < k$ moving $b_{i}$ past $b_{k}$ costs one sign from $v_{i}v_{k}$ and one from $v_{i}\pi_{i}$, so $b_{i}b_{k} = b_{k}b_{i}$. The check verifies the identities, and that the product of all steps is nonzero, for $N = 2, \dots, 6$ in $\Cl(0,0,2N)$, for $N = 3$ with six orthogonal null vectors of $\Cl(6,6)$, and for the Jordan-Wigner steps with $N = 2, 3$ in $\Cl(N,N)$.

\emph{(iv)} $Bl_{+} = e_{t}e_{r}e_{t} + e_{t}e_{r}e_{r} = -e_{r} - e_{t} = -l_{+}$ and $l_{+}B = e_{t}e_{t}e_{r} + e_{r}e_{t}e_{r} = e_{r} + e_{t} = l_{+}$, so $B$ anticommutes with $l_{+}$; for scalar $\alpha, \beta$, $\widetilde{R} = \alpha - \beta B$ and $l_{+}\widetilde{R} = Rl_{+}$, hence $Rl_{+}\widetilde{R} = R^{2}l_{+} = (\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta B)l_{+} = (\alpha - \beta)^{2}l_{+}$, and likewise $Rl_{-}\widetilde{R} = (\alpha + \beta)^{2}l_{-}$ since $Bl_{-} = l_{-}$. For the finite boost only $R^{2} = \cosh\phi + \sinh\phi\,B$ enters, with $\cosh\phi - \sinh\phi = \tfrac54 - \tfrac34 = \tfrac12$, $\cosh\phi + \sinh\phi = 2$ and $(\tfrac54)^{2} - (\tfrac34)^{2} = 1$. For the nilpotent rapidity, $d = s\rho_{1}\rho_{2}$ is even and built from generators orthogonal to $e_{t}, e_{r}$, so it commutes with them and $d^{2} = 0$; since $d$ is central in the subalgebra generated by $e_{t}, e_{r}, \rho_{1}, \rho_{2}$ with $d^{2} = 0$, $(dB)^{2} = 0$ and the series stops: $\exp(\pm\tfrac12 dB) = 1 \pm \tfrac12 dB$, mutually inverse. Computing directly, $(1 + \tfrac12 dB)\,l_{+}(1 - \tfrac12 dB) = (1 - \tfrac12 d)^{2}l_{+} = (1 - d)l_{+}$, using $Bl_{+} = -l_{+}$, $l_{+}B = l_{+}$; likewise $(1 + d)l_{-}$. The reversion of $\Cl(1,1,2)$ fixes $dB$ (grade $4$), so $\widetilde{R} = R$, $R\widetilde{R} = 1 + dB \ne 1$, and $Rl_{+}\widetilde{R} = l_{+}$: the boost is a boost of $\Cl(1,1)$ over $\R[d]/(d^{2})$ with $\R[d]$-linear reversion, not a rotor of $\Cl(1,1,2)$. The check verifies each identity for $s = 1, -3, \tfrac25$, the reversion statements, and the finite boost.

tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.formal: Let $A$ be a unital real algebra and $m \geq 1$. Then: (i) $Z(\Mat_m(A)) = Z(A)\cdot 1_m$; (ii) if $A$ is simple, so is $\Mat_m(A)$; (iii) $\Mat_m(\Mat_r(D)) \cong \Mat_{mr}(D)$ for any unital $D$; (iv) $\Mat_m(A_1 \oplus A_2) \cong \Mat_m(A_1) \oplus \Mat_m(A_2)$.
tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.technical:
For a unital real algebra $A$ and $m \geq 1$, passing to $m \times m$ matrices over $A$ preserves the basic structure. The centre is $Z(\Mat_m(A)) = Z(A) \cdot 1_m$; $\Mat_m(A)$ is simple whenever $A$ is; nested matrix algebras regroup, $\Mat_m(\Mat_r(D)) \cong \Mat_{mr}(D)$ for any unital $D$; and amplification distributes over direct sums, $\Mat_m(A_1 \oplus A_2) \cong \Mat_m(A_1) \oplus \Mat_m(A_2)$.

The first two statements follow from computations with the matrix units $E_{kl}$; the last two are regroupings of indices.
tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.lay: Replacing an algebra by square matrices whose entries come from that algebra changes its size but not its essential character. The centre stays the same, simplicity is kept, matrices of matrices are just larger matrices, and a direct sum of algebras splits into a direct sum of matrix algebras.
tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.typing_note: Self-contained computation with matrix units and no store references, so no edges.

proofs.main: Parts (i) and (ii) are \claimref{std-algebra.morita-amplification}(i) and (ii); the computation runs as follows. (i) Let $z = (z_{ij})$ be central. The entries of $z E_{kl} = E_{kl} z$ are $(z E_{kl})_{ij} = z_{ik}\,\delta_{lj}$ and $(E_{kl} z)_{ij} = \delta_{ik}\, z_{lj}$; equality for all $i, j, k, l$ forces $z_{ik} = 0$ for $i \neq k$ and $z_{kk} = z_{ll}$, so $z = a \cdot 1_m$ with $a := z_{11}$, and commuting with $b \cdot 1_m$ for all $b \in A$ forces $a \in Z(A)$. The converse inclusion is clear. transport.centre.formal: For $n \geq 1$, the centre of $\Cl(p,q)$ is $\R \cdot 1$ if $n$ is even, and $\R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$ if $n$ is odd, where $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$ is the pseudoscalar.
transport.centre.technical:
Let $n = p + q \geq 1$ and let $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$ be the pseudoscalar of $\Cl(p,q)$. The centre $\Zc$ of the algebra depends only on the parity of $n$: for even $n$ it is just the scalars, $\Zc = \R \cdot 1$, while for odd $n$ it is two-dimensional, $\Zc = \R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$.

The standard reason is that each basis blade either commutes or anticommutes with each generator $e_j$, and the only blades commuting with every generator are $1$ and, when $n$ is odd, $\omega$.
transport.centre.lay: The centre of an algebra is the set of its elements that commute with everything else in it. For the Clifford algebra of a space with an even number of dimensions, only the ordinary numbers do this. With an odd number of dimensions there is one more such element, the product of all the basis directions, so the centre becomes two-dimensional.

transport.classification-idempotent-orbi.technical:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate, so that by the classification $A \cong \Mat_m(D)$ or $\Mat_m(D) \oplus \Mat_m(D)$ with $D \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$, acting on $D^m$ (or a pair of copies). The rank of an idempotent is the $D$-dimension of its image, a rank pair in the split case. Two idempotents are conjugate under inner automorphisms if and only if they have the same rank data; in particular $e$ and $1 - e$ are conjugate if and only if $\mathrm{rank}\,e = m - \mathrm{rank}\,e$, componentwise in the split case.

An idempotent is central if and only if its conjugation orbit is a single point. This makes the boundary between obstruction types P and C orbit-theoretic: type C idempotents are those conjugation cannot move, type P those it moves through a full rank class.
transport.classification-idempotent-orbi.lay: Idempotents are elements equal to their own square, like projections onto a subspace. This result sorts them in any nondegenerate real Clifford algebra: two are related by an internal change of viewpoint exactly when they project onto subspaces of the same size (in each of the two blocks, when the algebra splits into two). The ones that no such change can move at all are exactly the ones that commute with everything, and this is how the series separates two of its types of obstruction.

proofs.main:
(1) Conjugation preserves rank, since $geg^{-1}$ has image $g(\mathrm{im}\, e)$. Conversely let $e, e'$ be idempotents of equal rank $r$ on $V = D^m$, on which $A \cong \Mat_m(D)$ acts (\claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}). Each splits $V$: $V = \mathrm{im}\,e \oplus \ker e$, both summands free (a finitely generated submodule of a free module over a division ring is free, with well-defined dimension); choose $D$-bases of $\mathrm{im}\,e$ and $\ker e$, and likewise for $e'$. The $D$-linear map $g$ carrying the first adapted basis to the second is invertible and satisfies $g e g^{-1} = e'$, both sides being the projection onto $g(\mathrm{im}\,e) = \mathrm{im}\,e'$ along $g(\ker e) = \ker e'$. In the split case, invertible elements are pairs of invertibles and conjugation acts componentwise (inner automorphisms preserve the two ideals, which are the algebra's minimal central summands), so the same argument applies in each slot and no inner automorphism exchanges slots.

(2) is (1) applied to the pair, $\mathrm{rank}(1-e) = m - \mathrm{rank}(e)$.

(3) If $e$ is central its orbit is $\{e\}$. Conversely, if $geg^{-1} = e$ for every invertible $g$, then $e$ commutes with every invertible element, hence with every sum of two of them, hence with all of $A$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.units-span}: $e$ is central. The identification of the singleton-orbit idempotents with the taxonomy's type C, and of the moved ones with type P, is then Definition \claimref{obj.transport.obstruction-types} read against (1).

transport.classification-real-clifford-a.formal:
Let $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$. Then $\Cl(p,q)$ is isomorphic, as a real associative algebra, to
\[
\begin{array}{llll}
d = 0:\ \Mat_{k}(\R), &
d = 1:\ \Mat_{k}(\R) \oplus \Mat_{k}(\R), &
d = 2:\ \Mat_{k}(\R), &
d = 3:\ \Mat_{k}(\C), \\[2pt]
d = 4:\ \Mat_{k}(\HH), &
d = 5:\ \Mat_{k}(\HH) \oplus \Mat_{k}(\HH), &
d = 6:\ \Mat_{k}(\HH), &
d = 7:\ \Mat_{k}(\C),
\end{array}
\]
with $k$ in each case determined by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$. In particular $\Cl(p,q)$ is a simple algebra except when $d \in \{1, 5\}$, i.e.\ except when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.
transport.classification-real-clifford-a.technical:
The real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ is, as a real associative algebra, a full matrix algebra over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, or a direct sum of two copies of one, and which case occurs depends only on $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$: $\Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 0, 2$; $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 1$; $\Mat_k(\C)$ for $d = 3, 7$; $\Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 4, 6$; and $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 5$. In each case the size $k$ is fixed by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$.

Consequently $\Cl(p,q)$ is a simple algebra except when $d \in \{1, 5\}$, that is when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.
transport.classification-real-clifford-a.lay: Clifford algebras built from a space with p positive and q negative directions turn out to be familiar objects in disguise: square tables of numbers (matrices) whose entries are real numbers, complex numbers or quaternions, or a pair of such tables side by side. Which of these appears depends only on p minus q, in a pattern that repeats every eight steps. Usually the algebra is a single indivisible block; it splits into two identical pieces exactly when p minus q leaves remainder 1 on division by four.

transport.corner-even-subalgebra.lay: When an algebra splits into two blocks, each block can be compared with the algebra's even part, built from products of an even number of directions. This result shows each block is an exact copy of that even part. It also shows that enlarging the algebra by one extra direction and then cutting back down to the block returns the same block.

But $\omega$ has odd grade ($n$ odd) while $a$ is even, so $\omega a$ is odd and $-a$ is even; a common value is possible only if both vanish, so $a = 0$. Surjectivity follows by dimension: $\dim \Cl^0 = 2^{n-1} = 	frac12 \dim A = \dim \varepsilon_+ A$ (the first equality is \claimref{std-algebra.z2-grading}), the last equality because $x \mapsto (\varepsilon_+ x, \varepsilon_- x)$ splits $A$ into two summands exchanged (linearly) by the grade involution, which maps $\varepsilon_+ x \mapsto \varepsilon_- \hat{x}$ and is bijective. u \varepsilon_+$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.decomposition-commutation}; the first term is $\varepsilon_+ A$ (centrality in $A$), and the second vanishes: $
u \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_- 
u$ (Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}), so $\varepsilon_+ a 
u \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_+ a \varepsilon_- 
u = (\varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_-) a 
u = 0$.

transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.formal: Let $n$ be odd and consider the two real forms of the Lorentzian algebra in dimension $n$, $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ (time of square $+1$) and $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ (time of square $-1$). Then $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type. The two real forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$, realised as $\Cl(V) \oplus \Cl(V)I_{\hat V}$ with $V$ the $n$-dimensional space and $I_{\hat V}$ the central pseudoscalar of the odd extension $\hat V$ of $V \oplus \R f$ ($f$ one further vector), which squares to $-1$ and commutes with every vector (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), the element $\omega' = \omega$ or $I_{\hat V}\omega$, whichever has square $+1$, is central, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are its central idempotents. Thus the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension; the real form decides whether it is visible as a splitting or hidden as a central complex structure.
transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.technical:
For odd $n$ compare the two Lorentzian real forms $\Cl(1,n-1)$, with $Q = +1$ on the time generator, and $\Cl(n-1,1)$, with $Q = -1$ on it. Using the commuting-square theorem on where the obstruction sits among one-dimensional extensions, $\Cl(1,n-1)$ is of type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n-1,1)$ is of type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type.

Both forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$, with complex unit $I_{\hat V}$, the central pseudoscalar of an odd extension of $V \oplus \R f$, whichever of $\omega$ and $I_{\hat V}\omega$ squares to $+1$ is a central involution $\omega'$, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are central idempotents. So the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension, and the real form decides whether it appears as a splitting or as a central complex structure.
transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.lay: In an odd number of spacetime dimensions there are two ways to set up the algebra, depending on whether time is given a positive or a negative square. transport.sign.formal: $\displaystyle \omega^2 = (-1)^{\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}} (-1)^q = (-1)^{\tfrac{(p-q)(p-q-1)}{2}}$. In particular $\omega^2 = +1$ if and only if $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
transport.sign.technical:
For the pseudoscalar $\omega = e_1 \cdots e_n$ of $\Cl(p,q)$, with $n = p + q$, the square is fixed by a count of signs: reversing the order of the $n$ generators costs $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, and $\omega$ times its reverse is the product of the $Q(e_i)$, which is $(-1)^q$. Hence $\omega^2 = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^q$.

This depends only on $p - q$, namely $\omega^2 = (-1)^{(p-q)(p-q-1)/2}$, and in particular $\omega^2 = +1$ exactly when $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
transport.sign.lay: Multiplying all the basis directions of a Clifford algebra together gives a special element called the pseudoscalar. Its square is always plus one or minus one, and this result says which. The answer depends only on the number of positive directions minus the number of negative ones: the square is plus one when that difference leaves remainder 0 or 1 on division by four, and minus one otherwise.
